content: The Joint Committee on Infant Hearing (JCIH) strongly advocates for the early detection and intervention of hearing loss in infants. The primary objective of Early Hearing Detection and Intervention (EHDI) programs is to optimize linguistic competence and literacy development in children who are deaf or hard of hearing. Without timely and appropriate language-learning opportunities, these children are at risk of falling behind their hearing peers in communication, cognitive development, reading, and social-emotional growth. Such delays can lead to lower educational and employment outcomes in adulthood. To achieve the best outcomes, all infants should undergo hearing screening by no later than one month of age. Infants who do not pass the initial screening should receive a comprehensive audiological evaluation by three months of age. Those with confirmed hearing loss should begin appropriate intervention services by six months of age, provided by healthcare and educational professionals with expertise in pediatric hearing loss and deafness. Regardless of the results of the initial hearing screening, all infants should receive ongoing monitoring of their communicative development starting at two months of age during well-child visits in their medical home. EHDI systems must ensure seamless transitions for infants and their families throughout the screening, diagnosis, and intervention process. The definition of targeted hearing loss has been expanded to include not only congenital permanent bilateral or unilateral sensory or conductive hearing loss but also neural hearing loss, such as auditory neuropathy/dyssynchrony, particularly in infants admitted to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU). Separate screening protocols are recommended for NICU and well-infant nurseries. NICU infants admitted for more than five days should have auditory brainstem response (ABR) testing included in their screening to detect neural hearing loss. Infants who fail automated ABR testing in the NICU should be referred directly to an audiologist for rescreening and, if necessary, a comprehensive evaluation including ABR. For rescreening, a complete evaluation of both ears is recommended, even if only one ear failed the initial screening. Infants readmitted to the hospital within the first month of life, particularly those with conditions associated with potential hearing loss (e.g., hyperbilirubinemia requiring exchange transfusion or culture-positive sepsis), should undergo repeat hearing screening before discharge. Audiologists with expertise in evaluating newborns and young infants with hearing loss should provide diagnostic audiology services, including auditory habilitation and the selection and fitting of amplification devices. At least one ABR test is recommended as part of a complete audiological evaluation for children under three years of age to confirm permanent hearing loss. The frequency and timing of hearing reevaluations for children with risk factors should be individualized based on the likelihood of delayed-onset hearing loss. Infants who pass the neonatal screening but have risk factors should have at least one diagnostic audiology assessment by 24 to 30 months of age. Earlier and more frequent assessments may be necessary for children with conditions such as cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, syndromes associated with progressive hearing loss, neurodegenerative disorders, trauma, or culture-positive postnatal infections linked to sensorineural hearing loss. Children who have undergone extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) or chemotherapy, or those with caregiver concerns or a family history of hearing loss, may also require closer monitoring. For families choosing amplification, infants diagnosed with permanent hearing loss should be fitted with an amplification device within one month of diagnosis. Infants with confirmed hearing loss should also be offered a genetics consultation, evaluated by an otolaryngologist with expertise in pediatric hearing loss, and undergo at least one visual acuity assessment by an ophthalmologist experienced in evaluating infants. Risk factors for congenital and acquired hearing loss have been consolidated into a single list rather than being grouped by the time of onset. All families of infants with any degree of bilateral or unilateral permanent hearing loss should be eligible for early intervention services. Central referral points should be established to ensure access to specialized services for infants with confirmed hearing loss. Early intervention services should be provided by professionals with expertise in hearing loss, including educators of the deaf, speech-language pathologists, and audiologists. Both home-based and center-based intervention options should be available to families. Regular developmental surveillance, including auditory skills, parental concerns, and middle-ear status, should be conducted in the medical home in accordance with the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) periodicity schedule. Standardized developmental screenings using validated tools should occur at 9, 18, and 24 to 30 months of age, or whenever concerns arise. Infants who fail the speech-language portion of a global screening or for whom there are concerns about hearing or language should be referred for speech-language evaluation and audiological assessment. Birth hospitals, in collaboration with state EHDI coordinators, must ensure that hearing screening results are communicated to parents and the medical home. Parents should receive appropriate follow-up and resource information, and hospitals should ensure that each infant is linked to a medical home. Information at all stages of the EHDI process should be conveyed to families in a culturally sensitive and understandable format. Individual hearing screening, audiology diagnostic, and habilitation information should be promptly transmitted to the medical home and state EHDI coordinator. Families should be informed of all communication options and available hearing technologies in an unbiased manner, allowing informed family choice to guide decision-making. States should implement data-management and tracking systems as part of an integrated child health information system to monitor the quality of EHDI services and provide recommendations for system improvements. Effective collaboration between health and education professionals is essential to ensure successful transitions and to determine outcomes for children with hearing loss, aiding in public health policy planning. Unidentified hearing loss at birth can negatively impact speech, language, academic achievement, and social-emotional development. Historically, moderate-to-severe hearing loss in young children was often not detected until well beyond the newborn period, with milder or unilateral hearing loss frequently diagnosed only at school age. Advances in screening technology and the implementation of universal newborn hearing screening (UNHS) programs have significantly improved early identification and intervention. By 2005, approximately 95% of newborns in the United States were screened for hearing loss before hospital discharge. Early identification and intervention by six months of age have been shown to improve school-related outcomes, including vocabulary, articulation, intelligibility, social adjustment, and behavior. Despite these advancements, challenges remain, including the need for culturally sensitive communication with families, integrated state data systems, and sufficient facilities and personnel to provide follow-up services. Strengthening follow-up and intervention remains a priority for EHDI programs. All children with hearing loss should have access to resources necessary to reach their maximum potential. EHDI systems should be family-centered, ensuring informed choice, shared decision-making, and parental consent in accordance with state and federal guidelines. Families should have access to information about all intervention and treatment options, as well as counseling regarding hearing loss. The success of EHDI programs depends on collaboration among families, healthcare professionals, and educators. Each team member's role should be clearly defined and understood. Essential team members include birth hospitals, families, pediatricians or primary healthcare professionals, audiologists, otolaryngologists, speech-language pathologists, educators of the deaf or hard of hearing, and other early intervention professionals. Additional services, such as genetics, ophthalmology, developmental pediatrics, service coordination, and family education, should also be available. Audiologists play a critical role in EHDI programs, providing newborn hearing screening program development, management, quality assessment, and coordination of audiological diagnosis and treatment. They ensure timely fitting and monitoring of amplification devices and facilitate referrals to early intervention programs. Otolaryngologists determine the etiology of hearing loss, identify related risk indicators, and evaluate and treat ear diseases. Early intervention professionals, trained in various disciplines, provide specialized services to support the development of auditory, speech, and language skills. Families are central to the success of EHDI programs. They provide love, nurture, and communication for their infants, advocate for their needs, and participate in early intervention appointments. Families benefit from involvement with support groups, mentors, and the deaf and hard-of-hearing community, gaining knowledge and resources to support their child's development. Over time, children learn from their families' advocacy and develop independence and self-advocacy skills. A successful EHDI program requires collaboration among public and private institutions and agencies, with clearly defined roles and responsibilities. Each state should have a lead coordinating agency responsible for identifying funding sources and overseeing the development and implementation of EHDI systems. Multidisciplinary teams, including audiologists, physicians, and nursing personnel, are essential to establishing high-quality UNHS programs.
